This is Euler's polynomial, which famously produces primes for n = 0..39, but fails at n = 40: 40^2 + 40 + 41 = 1600 + 40 + 41 = 1681 = 41^2. So n = 40, d = 41. Let me verify: 40^2 = 1600; 1600 + 40 = 1640; 1640 + 41 = 1681. 41^2 = 1681. Yes, 41 is a proper divisor of 1681 (41 < 1681, 41 divides 1681 exactly since 1681/41 = 41). Also note the algebraic identity: n^2 + n + 41 at n = 41m gives... Actually the general factorization trick: f(n) = n^2 + n + 41, f(40) = 41^2. Also f(41k - 1)... f(40) = 41^2, and more generally f(41k - 1) is divisible by 41? Let's check: f(n) mod 41 = n^2 + n = n(n+1) mod 41. So f(n) ≡ 0 mod 41 when n ≡ 0 or n ≡ -1 (mod 41). n = 40 ≡ -1 mod 41, so f(40) ≡ 0 mod 41, and f(40) = 1681 = 41^2 > 41, hence composite. The JSON certificate: {" 	}
